intro: A judo jacket, a pair of boxing gloves, a fencing mask, a berimbau, an arnis stick and a mixed martial arts bout sheet can sit on one shelf. Each came from a different place and a different institution. Each has its own founding dates, governing bodies and rule books. This unit asks how to sort and compare them fairly.

First you will sort arts into six working groups: grappling, striking, armed arts made into sport, arts shaped by music and circle, diaspora arts and the modern mix. You will meet the institutions that draw these lines, from the IOC to UNESCO. Then you will compare two arts, judo and taekwondo, by origin, room, nation and code, with capoeira and boxing as a second pair.

By the end, you can explain why a taxonomy is a tool and not a ranking. You can name the laws, federations and dates behind each art. You can also write a comparison that cites its records and marks where legend ends and the documents begin.
bigQuestion: How can we compare martial arts by their rooms, nations and rule books without ranking one above another?

timeline.t: Greek records say pankration joins the ancient Olympic Games
Carl Linnaeus publishes Systema Naturae, a model for sorting by named groups
The Queensberry Rules for boxing are published in London
Kanō Jigorō opens the Kodokan at Eishō-ji temple in Tokyo
Brazil's Penal Code makes practicing capoeira in public a crime
The FIE, the world fencing body, is founded in Paris
The International Judo Federation is founded
The name taekwondo is chosen in South Korea
Judo becomes an Olympic sport at Tokyo
The first UFC event is held in Denver, Colorado
Republic Act No. 9850 names arnis the national martial art of the Philippines
UNESCO lists the capoeira circle as intangible cultural heritage

words.d: a system for sorting things into named groups by shared features
the single test used to decide which group something belongs in
an order from best to worst on one scale
arts whose contests are decided by gripping and controlling rather than by hitting
arts whose contests are scored mainly by landing blows
a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
living practices that communities pass down; UNESCO keeps lists of them
an organization of national bodies that writes the rules for a sport
a government board that licenses athletes and approves events
a record made at the time, such as a law, a police record or a founder's writing
an old story that people tell, which may not be a documented event
one version of a rule book, marked by a number or a year

test.q: What makes a taxonomy different from a ranking?
choices: A taxonomy sorts into groups by shared features; a ranking orders from best to worst.
A taxonomy lists only Olympic sports.
test.why: A taxonomy groups things side by side; a ranking puts them in order on one scale.

test.q: What was the first UFC event, held in Denver in 1993, promoted as?
choices: a test of which style was best
test.why: Promoters sold UFC 1 as a contest of styles; historians note it tested eight people under one rule set.

test.q: Which art did UNESCO list in 2014?
test.why: UNESCO listed the capoeira circle of Brazil in 2014.
United World Wrestling, founded in 1912 and renamed in 2014, governs Olympic wrestling.

test.q: Which art allowed both holding and hitting at the ancient Olympics?
test.why: Pankration, added in 648 BCE, allowed both.

test.q: What did Republic Act No. 9850 of 2009 do?
choices: It named arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines.
test.why: The Philippine law named arnis the national martial art and sport and brought it into schools.

test.q: Which people brought pencak silat to the Netherlands?
choices: Indo-Dutch families after Indonesian independence in 1949
test.why: Indo-Dutch families who moved after 1949 carried pencak silat to the Netherlands.

test.q: Which body adopted the Unified Rules of mixed martial arts in 2009?
test.why: The Association of Boxing Commissions adopted the Unified Rules, first drafted in New Jersey.

test.q: Where did Kanō Jigorō open the Kodokan in 1882?
choices: at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo
test.why: The Kodokan began in a small room at Eishō-ji temple in Tokyo.

test.q: What did Brazil's Penal Code of 1890 do?
choices: It made practicing capoeira in public a crime.
It sent capoeira to the Olympics.
test.why: The 1890 Penal Code banned public capoeira, two years after abolition in 1888.

test.q: Who founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation in 1966?
test.why: General Choi Hong-hi founded the ITF in 1966.

test.q: In taekwondo, which body grants dan certificates?
test.why: The Kukkiwon grants dan certificates; World Taekwondo writes competition rules.

test.q: When did women's judo become an Olympic medal event?
test.why: Women's judo was a demonstration in 1988 and a medal event from 1992.

test.q: What did Allen Guttmann's From Ritual to Record (1978) offer historians?
choices: a ranking of the best martial arts
seven named features of modern sport for comparison
test.why: Guttmann listed seven features, such as bureaucracy and quantification, without ranking sports.

test.q: Why must a historian name a rule book's edition?
choices: Rules change, as the blue judogi and electronic scoring show.
test.why: Rules are revised, so a claim is only true for a given edition and year.

write.prompt: Choose two martial arts from this unit. Compare them by origin, room, nation and code without ranking them. Cite at least three named records, such as a law, a founding date, a federation's rules or an Olympic result, with their years.
tips: Name each record you cite and give its year, such as the Penal Code of 1890 or Republic Act No. 9850.
Set legends beside records and label which is which.
Say which criterion you are using before you sort or compare.
Compare what each institution does; do not judge which art is better.
Use the unit's terms, such as federation, diaspora and edition.
